say.text: On the ward, a consultant asks for the one numeric cut-off that makes acute cholecystitis TG18 Grade II (moderate).
Which do you pick?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Grade II means inflammation that has already turned moderate, so the white count has to clear well above the everyday infection flag. Which number did TG18 set?
Yes. TG18 Grade II is any one of: WBC above 18,000/mm³, a tender palpable RUQ mass, complaints over 72 hours, or marked local inflammation.
The cut-offs are set for this grading, not for routine sepsis flags, so the everyday numbers do not grade the disease.
That is not right.
It tempts because a white count of 10,000 is the familiar infection flag you meet everywhere.
TG18 sets its own white-count threshold for Grade II, so the everyday flag does not decide the grade. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix this one first: the everyday flag is the reflex that grades the disease wrongly.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts because a day of pain sounds like a long, worrying course, and 24 hours is a figure you carry around.
Grade II uses duration too, but on a much longer scale than a day. Look at what the grade actually counts. Try again.
Now Grade III, severe. One failing organ system is enough, so which single cut-off is a TG18 criterion?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Grade III is about failing organs, not borderline lab values. Ask which single organ number is clearly abnormal, well past the routine flag.
That is not right.
It tempts because a creatinine of 1.5 is the value that prompts a repeat test, so it feels severe.
The TG18 renal criterion needs a clear fall in function, not a borderline rise, so a mild rise does not qualify. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Renal numbers decide Grade III, so recheck the threshold before you grade a patient.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts because the INR is the number you use for warfarin, so a slightly raised value feels like organ failure.
The TG18 liver criterion is a clearly raised INR, not a mild elevation, so a value this close to normal does not grade the disease. Try again.
Yes. Grade III is organ dysfunction in any one system, and the renal line you picked is one of them.
The other systems: dopamine at 5 µg/kg/min or any noradrenaline; reduced consciousness; PaO2/FiO2 below 300; PT-INR above 1.5; platelets below 100,000/mm³.
Think one organ is enough: a single failing system makes the whole episode Grade III.
A 68-year-old man with acute cholecystitis is on noradrenaline for low blood pressure. His creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL.
Your first move?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with how many organs are failing. That answer decides whether the operation can come first at all.
That is not right.
It tempts because early keyhole surgery is the standard for the fit patient you usually see, so it comes to mind by reflex.
This man has failing organs, and organ failure sets the order. Operating before the organs are supported adds risk. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure. This reflex is the one that most often goes wrong in a sick patient, so check the organs first.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts because a very sick-looking patient seems to need the whole gallbladder out at once.
The operation type is not the question; the organ state decides whether surgery is safe at all. Try again.
Yes. In Grade III, organ support comes first, and in most patients gallbladder drainage comes before any surgery.
Drainage is done by percutaneous cholecystostomy in patients too ill for surgery, and early surgery is kept for selected fit patients.
You have just seen that in Grade III the gallbladder is drained before any operation. Which explanation fits?

choices.label: The 72 hour window has already closed
Drainage cures the disease, so no operation is needed
Surgery is unsafe while organs fail; support and drain first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a failing organ does to the safety of an operation, then ask what that means for the order of steps.
That is not right.
It tempts because the 72-hour mark is the ideal window for early surgery, so a missed window sounds like a closed door.
The 72-hour mark is the best time for early surgery, not a deadline that bars it, and it does not explain the drain-first order. Try again.
That is not right.
It tempts because pus draining from the gallbladder looks like the infection being removed.
Drainage is a bridge for patients too ill for surgery; it relieves the sepsis but does not settle the gallbladder for good. Try again.
Yes. Surgery in a patient with failing organs carries too much risk, so support and gallbladder drainage come first.
Early surgery is kept for the selected fit patients, treated at advanced centres.
Exam question: the treatment of choice for acute calculous cholecystitis in a fit patient, by current standards?

choices.label: Conservative treatment, then interval cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the current evidence says about hospital stay and complications for a fit patient, and what the older books were built around.
That is not right for current practice.
It tempts because the settle-first, operate-at-six-to-eight-weeks plan is the one most older exam keys have printed.
Teach both: that was the expected answer in older question papers, but it is no longer the standard for a fit patient. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Many revision books still print the older key, so recheck it against the current standard.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts because drainage is the step you have just seen, so it feels like the first move for any sick gallbladder.
Drainage is kept for patients too ill for surgery. This question is about a fit patient in the index admission. Try again.
Yes. For a fit patient the current choice is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission, ideally within 72 hours.
Older PYQs expected the interval route, but early surgery shortens total stay without more complications or conversion.
A fit patient with mild disease, 48 hours of symptoms, is admitted. What is your plan?

choices.label: Discharge on antibiotics, operate after 6-8 weeks
Wait for the pain to settle before booking surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether this fit patient needs anything before the operation, and whether waiting is what current practice asks for.
That is not right.
It tempts because discharge on antibiotics with a later operation is the plan many textbooks still describe.
That is the traditional alternative, which current practice has moved away from for a fit patient. Try again.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check whether your plan leaves this fit patient in hospital longer than it needs to be.

say.text: That is not right.
It tempts because inflamed tissue sounds as if it must cool before anyone operates on it.
Cooling first is the old reason for interval surgery, a reason current practice has set aside for a fit patient. Try again.
Yes. A fit patient with mild disease gets early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission, which shortens stay without more complications.
The rule to keep: grade and fitness set the timing and the route, and the stone alone does not force a wait.
